summary: Specifies an experimental TLS 1.3 extension that lets a server authenticate using both a certificate and an external pre-shared key. It was replaced by RFC 9973.

eli5.summary: To get in, you show your ID card and also say a secret password. Using both makes it harder for a fake to get in.

what is the tls external psk authentication extension
how does the cert with extern psk extension protect against quantum computers

subtitle: Combine a certificate and secret key in TLS 1.3 to protect against quantum threats

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 uses key agreement and signature algorithms vulnerable to future quantum computers. An attacker storing today's encrypted TLS traffic could decrypt it later if quantum computers become available.
tldr.mechanism: This extension lets servers authenticate using both a certificate (as usual) and an external pre-shared key (a strong secret), both contributing to the key schedule. The PSK adds quantum-resistant protection even if the handshake algorithms are broken later.
tldr.outcome: Sessions are protected against future quantum decryption without sacrificing today's certificate-based authentication. RFC 9973 superseded this experimental approach with a more mature standard.

today: RFC 8773 is an Experimental RFC. RFC 9973 superseded this extension with a more refined approach.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 currently provides two separate ways for a server to prove its identity: with a certificate and digital signature, or with a pre-shared key (a secret established beforehand). This extension allows both at the same time. A server can authenticate with a certificate while also using an external pre-shared key as input to the TLS key derivation. The external PSK does not replace certificate authentication; it enhances it.

This document defines an Experimental Protocol. Several implementers wanted to test this idea before standardizing it, so it was published to enable real-world implementations and deployment experience.
sections.eli5: Normally, TLS picks one way to prove who you are: show a certificate OR say a secret password. This extension lets you do both at once, which is safer.

sections.title: Protecting Against Quantum Threats
sections.content:
A large-scale quantum computer would break the cryptographic algorithms TLS 1.3 relies on today, including RSA and ECDSA for signatures and Diffie-Hellman for key agreement. It is unknown whether or when such a computer will exist, but if one is built, an attacker who recorded encrypted TLS sessions today could decrypt them in the future. This is called a "harvest now, decrypt later" attack.

This extension protects against that threat by incorporating an external pre-shared key into the key schedule. If the external PSK is secure, and if the key derivation algorithm remains unbroken, the session secrets are protected even if an attacker later breaks the signature and key agreement algorithms. The certificate authentication mechanism itself is unchanged, so existing trust models remain intact.
sections.eli5: Someone could record all your secret messages today, then use a future quantum computer to decode them. Adding a strong secret password now protects those old messages even if quantum computers break the normal math later.

sections.title: How the Extension Works
sections.content:
When a client wants to use this extension, it includes the tls_cert_with_extern_psk extension in its ClientHello message. The client must also send the key_share, psk_key_exchange_modes, and pre_shared_key extensions. The extension must not be used with early data (early_data extension).

If the server accepts, it includes the extension in the ServerHello and selects one of the external PSKs offered by the client. The server must possess that PSK and be willing to perform certificate-based authentication. When successfully negotiated, both the external PSK and the ECDH shared secret contribute to the Early Secret, Handshake Secret, and Master Secret in the TLS 1.3 key schedule. Authentication via certificate and signature is unchanged.
sections.eli5: The client says "I can prove I am me with a certificate AND this secret password." If the server agrees and has that password, they both use both proofs to create the session encryption key.

sections.title: Authentication with Certificates and Keys
sections.content:
When the extension is negotiated, the server sends its Certificate and CertificateVerify messages as usual, proving it possesses the private key matching its certificate. TLS 1.3 normally prevents client certificate authentication when a PSK is used, but this extension removes that restriction. If certificate-based client authentication is desired, the client can now send its own Certificate and CertificateVerify messages.

The external PSK itself is not used for authentication; it is used only as input to the key derivation. Authentication is based entirely on the public key certificates and digital signatures, as in standard TLS 1.3. If the external PSK is compromised and known to other parties, the authentication cannot be forged because authentication depends on the private keys, not the PSK.
sections.eli5: The secret password does not prove who you are; the ID card does. The password just scrambles the session encryption in a way that even a quantum computer cannot unscramble if it does not know the password.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the external PSK with secure key-generation and management techniques, such as pseudorandom generation or derivation from other secure keys. Weak random number generators can produce guessable PSKs that are easier for an attacker to search than the full key space. Implementations must generate external PSKs with sufficient entropy and manage them securely throughout their lifetime.

If the external PSK becomes known to parties other than the client and server, it must not be the sole basis for authentication. Since this extension requires certificate-based authentication, this requirement is satisfied: knowledge of the PSK does not enable impersonation because the attacker still does not possess the private key. However, implementers should not transmit the same content on both a PSK-protected connection and an unprotected connection, as this allows eavesdroppers to correlate the connections.
sections.eli5: Keep the secret password safe. If someone learns it, they still cannot pretend to be you because they do not have your private ID. But do not use the same password for things you want to keep secret and things you do not.
